name: copy-on-write
intent: Let several handles of a value share one expensive body until the first write, which clones that body privately, so copying costs a pointer instead of a deep copy while every handle still behaves as an independent value.
problem: A value with an expensive body (large buffer, collection, tree, document) is copied eagerly on assignment, argument passing and return even though most copies are never modified: time and memory are spent duplicating data that would have stayed identical. The naive fix - handing out one mutable object behind several handles - breaks the copy contract, and unrelated parts of the program then observe each other's writes.
context: Applies when copies of an expensive payload vastly outnumber modifications, when the payload is large enough that the copy dominates the cost of the handle (multi-kilobyte buffers, collection snapshots, editor or model state), and when the language offers a cheap way to know whether the body is still shared - a reference count, an explicit shared flag, or a uniqueness test. It is a single-threaded optimization first; sharing the count across threads turns it into the separate thread-safe copy-on-write concern.
benefits: Copying becomes O(1): assignment, parameter passing, container insertion and return values move a handle and bump a count instead of duplicating the body.

Memory use collapses when many copies differ little or are never written - the classic case of a large payload passed by value through several layers (Qt implicit sharing, pre-C++11 std::string, OS fork page sharing).
Value semantics survive: the caller still sees an independent object, and no aliasing bug can appear as long as every mutator detaches before it writes.

Reads are safe to share without synchronization while the body stays immutable between writes, which is why snapshot containers (CopyOnWriteArrayList) and immutable snapshots publish cheaply across threads.
Readers and iterators keep the body they started with, so traversal is never invalidated by a concurrent write and never throws concurrent-modification errors.
The same share-until-write idea scales up to object graphs: persistent collections, immutable update trees and functional new-version state are its structural-sharing descendants.

Fork-based snapshots (Redis BGSAVE, database consistent backups) get a point-in-time memory image at near-zero cost; the child sees a frozen view while the parent continues mutating pages, with only the written pages duplicated.

Filesystem snapshots (ZFS, Btrfs) and database MVCC (Postgres, LMDB) are applications of the same share-until-write principle at disk-block and row-version granularity respectively, making snapshots O(1) and eliminating torn-write risk without journaling.

COW B-trees (LMDB, Btrfs) provide natural MVCC snapshot isolation: readers traversing an old root never block and see a consistent point-in-time view without acquiring latches, because the old tree is never modified.

Swift's Array, String, Dictionary, Set, and Data all use COW with isKnownUniquelyReferenced() uniqueness checks at compile/runtime, making value-type copies effectively free in the common read-only case.
tradeoffs: The write path gets slower and more complex: every mutator must consult the sharing state and, on the first write, allocate and copy the whole body - worst-case latency spikes exactly where interactive code notices it.
A single missed detach is silent data corruption, not a crash: one mutator that forgets to detach rewrites the body another handle still believes it owns, and the bug surfaces far from its cause.

Interior references (an operator[] result, an iterator, a pointer into the body) either dangle or illegally share state after a detach, so implementations must mark an object unshareable the moment such a reference escapes - the failure mode is data corruption, as in the classic example where a saved character reference makes the copy mutate the original.
The count is a concurrency hazard: non-atomic read-modify-write races either lose a detach or double-free, and atomic increments on a hot shared body ping-pong cache lines and cap scalability.

Sharing becomes observable: identity and pointer equality, iterator freshness and snapshot semantics change, so code that relied on 'reference means live object' or on seeing every update breaks in subtle ways.

Not every runtime can detect sharing: without deterministic destruction or a uniqueness test (plain Python, Ruby, Go objects) the sharing state must be tracked by hand or the body copied defensively, which costs more than the copy it was meant to avoid.

A shared body lives as long as its longest-lived handle, so abandoning a large value in one place may retain the whole buffer; and once writes stop being rare, the count check, the clone and the bookkeeping are pure overhead on top of a copy that would have been cheaper up front.

Write amplification in COW filesystems and COW B-trees: modifying one leaf requires rewriting every node on the path to the root, multiplying I/O for small random updates (ZFS, Btrfs, LMDB). Systems mitigate this through write batching: accumulating multiple updates and applying them in a single root-to-leaf sweep amortizes path-copy cost across many mutations.
Memory pressure after fork(): a write-heavy parent during BGSAVE can transiently approach 2x RSS as every written page COW-faults into the child; Redis is the canonical example.
Fork page-table overhead: fork() copies page-table entries proportional to virtual address space size, not RSS; for large sparse processes this dominates even before the first COW fault.

GC + COW interaction: mark-and-sweep collectors that touch every object dirty every shared page, causing forked Python/Java/JS workers to copy nearly their entire heap on the next GC cycle even when doing no actual work.
THP (Transparent Huge Pages) inflates COW granularity: with 2MB pages instead of 4KB, a single byte write triggers a 2MB copy (512x amplification). Redis and other forking workloads must disable THP.

MADV_WIPEONFORK is required for security-sensitive post-fork data wiping (PRNG seeds, cryptographic secrets), but only works on private anonymous memory and cannot be applied to file-backed or shared mappings.

participants.responsibility: The small, freely copyable value clients see; it holds the (possibly shared) reference to the body and carries the sharing state that decides whether a write may happen in place.
The expensive representation - buffer, collection, tree, document state - whose contents are visible to every handle currently attached to it.
Reports how many handles reference the body (reference count, shared flag, intrusive counter, or a runtime uniqueness check); it is the only input to the detach decision.
The clone-on-first-write operation: allocate a private copy of the body, clone its contents, rebind the handle and release the old reference so the other holders keep their value.
Performs the logically mutating operation through the handle so the detach can run first, and must not retain interior references into the body across that boundary.

use_cases: Large buffers passed by value through API layers: strings, byte arrays and image/document payloads whose copies are usually read-only (Qt QString/QByteArray implicit sharing, ATL CString, pre-C++11 std::string).

Read-mostly collections whose traversals vastly outnumber mutations and must not block readers: listener and handler registries, routing tables, RuleEngine rule sets (CopyOnWriteArrayList/CopyOnWriteArraySet).
Configuration and state snapshots swapped atomically at the write boundary (feature flags, reloaded settings, event-sourced folds) so readers keep a consistent version without locking.

Persistent and functional data structures where an update returns a new version that structurally shares everything the change did not touch (Scala immutable collections, Immer drafts, persistent lists and maps).
Operating-system and memory-mapped sharing: fork and page-level copy-on-write share physical pages until a mapping is written, and file-backed buffers are shared until modified.
Columnar and data-frame workloads where slices are views and only the columns actually written are duplicated (pandas copy-on-write mode, Arrow buffers).

Fork-based process snapshots: Redis BGSAVE/BGREWRITEAOF forks a child to serialize memory to disk while the parent continues serving writes; only pages modified by the parent after fork are COW-copied, keeping the child's view consistent (vm.overcommit_memory=1 recommended).

COW filesystems for instant snapshots: ZFS and Btrfs never overwrite blocks in place; creating a snapshot is O(1) — save the root block pointer; reclaims O(1) more when the snapshot is deleted and no other reference remains. Enables self-healing via checksum propagation and efficient incremental replication via zfs send / btrfs send.

Database MVCC at row granularity: Postgres, LMDB, CockroachDB Pebble write new row versions on UPDATE/DELETE and reclaim old versions via VACUUM once no active transaction can see them; readers see consistent snapshots without read locks.

Container image layering: Docker/OCI images use layered COW where lower layers are read-only and the upper layer copies on write; base images are shared across many containers until a layer is actually modified.
APFS reflinks and XFS/ref ext4 ioctl(FICLONE): file-level COW that shares extents until either fork writes, enabling instant file clones (e.g., `cp --reflink=auto`) at near-zero cost.

LMDB's single-level store: a CoW B+tree using two fixed root pages (double buffering) where readers are fully latch-free and writers never block readers; no WAL needed because old trees remain intact until the new root is durably synced.

Swift standard library collections (Array, Dictionary, Set, String, Data) where isKnownUniquelyReferenced() checks the heap object's strong reference count at runtime to decide whether to mutate in-place or clone.

Qt QSharedData/QSharedDataPointer: implicit sharing for pimpl'd d-pointer classes where non-const operator-> triggers detach() automatically before any write access; QExplicitlySharedDataPointer suppresses automatic detach.

Rust std::borrow::Cow: a generic enum (Borrowed | Owned) that defers the clone until to_mut() is called, especially useful in APIs that accept both borrowed and owned data without multiple signatures.

PHP arrays and strings: reference-counted value types where assignment and argument passing share the zval and the first write 'separates' it (copy-on-write) when refcount > 1; taking a reference with & turns the sharing into an explicit alias set (php.net reference counting, php-src core docs).

pandas 3.0, where copy-on-write is the default and only mode: any DataFrame or Series derived by indexing behaves as an independent copy, chained assignment (df["foo"][mask] = v) silently doing nothing is eliminated - it raises ChainedAssignmentError - and every update must be a single .loc step (PDEP-7).

Linux kernel OverlayFS copy_up: a container write to a lowerdir file (open for write or metadata change) copies the file up into upperdir first; the metacopy feature delays the data copy until the first data write, and an fsync before the finalizing rename guards against zero-filled files after a crash (kernel overlayfs docs, Docker overlay2 driver).
avoid_when: Writes are as frequent as copies: copy eagerly, or keep one mutable object under a lock - a detach would run on nearly every operation and the sharing bookkeeping buys nothing.
The payload is small (a few words): the pointer, count and branch cost more than simply copying the value.
Readers must observe later writes through references they already hold, or iterators must stay live - snapshot semantics are wrong here; use a shared mutable structure with proper synchronization.

The elements are themselves handles or immutable references: a shallow copy is already O(1), so wrapping them in a copy-on-write layer adds indirection and counting for no gain (the reason C++11 forbade copy-on-write std::string and standard containers must copy their elements).

The runtime cannot tell whether the body is shared and no explicit flag is maintained (plain Python/Ruby/Go objects): track ownership explicitly or copy at the write edge instead of pretending to detect sharing.

The language already gives value semantics by default (Swift arrays and dictionaries, Scala immutable collections, Rust Cow/Arc::make_mut): use the runtime mechanism rather than hand-rolling a second layer with its own bugs.

Write-intensive random updates on COW filesystems: databases doing small random I/O on ZFS/Btrfs fragment heavily; set recordsize to match DB page size on ZFS, or use chattr +C (nodatacow) on Btrfs at the cost of losing checksumming and snapshot protection for those files.

Fork + exec is not needed: if a child process immediately execs, use posix_spawn() or ensure fork() is followed by exec() before touching memory; otherwise vfork() or CLONE_VM sharing is more appropriate than COW fork.

Multithreaded processes with hot refcount: every detach check on a shared body incurs atomic increments on the refcount; for very high-frequency updates in a thread pool, consider Arc::try_make_mut (Rust) or equivalent uniqueness-test APIs to avoid cache-line ping-pong.

Long-lived read transactions with MVCC COW stores (LMDB): if a reader holds a transaction open across many writes, the old versions cannot be reclaimed and the DB file grows toward 2x until the reader closes, devolving into append-only behavior.
KSM-merging sensitive workloads: MADV_MERGEABLE regions undergo regular scanning; if pages are frequently modified the merge/unmerge cycle overhead can exceed the savings from deduplication.
anti_patterns: Sharing one mutable object and calling it copy-on-write: real copy-on-write clones on the first write, so the other holders never see the change; 'share, then mutate in place' is plain aliasing with a nicer name.
Detaching in every accessor, including reads, so the copy is paid on the read path and the pattern becomes a pure loss.
Treating the count as truth across threads (non-atomic read-modify-write) - a race that loses a detach or frees the body twice.

Handing out interior references (iterators, operator[] results, pointers into the body) from a copy-on-write type without an unshareable state, so a later write silently changes what the caller already holds.
Applying copy-on-write to elements that are already handles or immutable, adding a second layer of indirection and counting where a plain copy was free.
Using copy-on-write to avoid designing ownership policy: reference cycles, retained bodies and unshareable objects accumulate until the performance win is negative.
Forking a process with an active mark-and-sweep GC without understanding that the next GC cycle will COW-copy nearly the entire heap.

Relying on isKnownUniquelyReferenced without thread synchronization and then mutating from multiple threads: the check is not guaranteed to be atomic across threads and two concurrent mutations can each see unique, proceed in-place, and overwrite each other's changes.
Using COW for write-heavy workloads where every mutation pays the detach+clone overhead plus the bookkeeping overhead on reads, resulting in worse performance than simple eager copy.
design_principles: Value semantics with shared representation: copies must behave as independent values, so sharing stays an implementation detail hidden behind the interface.
Lazy work: perform the copy when the write needs it, not when the possibility of a write appears.
Single responsibility per role: the handle owns the sharing decision, the body owns the data, the detach step owns the clone.
Separation of concerns: keep the sharing policy (plain count, atomics, lock, uniqueness test) independent of the data structure being shared.
Optimization behind a stable interface: the copy-on-write value must be usable exactly like the plain value so it can be removed without touching clients.
Zero-cost abstraction at read time: reads must never pay for the sharing machinery; detach cost is paid only by the first writer.
No interior reference escape: the body must be unreferenced from the outside, or the object must be marked unshareable the moment a reference escapes, to prevent dangling references after detach.
Snapshot semantics by default: readers and iterators receive a stable view that is unaffected by subsequent writes; this must be explicitly documented as the contract.
best_practices: Detach in one place per type - a private detach()/make_mut()/beginCOWMutation() helper called first by every mutator - never inline clone logic at call sites.

Prefer the language's own uniqueness test over a hand-rolled counter: shared_ptr use_count in single-threaded code, Swift's isKnownUniquelyReferenced, Rust Cow/Arc::make_mut, Qt QSharedDataPointer, ImmutableInterlocked for published immutable values.
Keep the body immutable from the outside: expose only const/read-only views, hand out no interior references, and mark the object unshareable the moment a reference escapes.
For cross-thread sharing use atomic counts or an immutable-snapshot swap (atomic.Pointer/atomic.Value, ImmutableInterlocked, a volatile final reference) rather than a plain integer.
Measure before keeping it: introduce copy-on-write only where reads dominate writes, and keep the plain value type behind the same interface for comparison.
Document the aliasing contract: iterators are snapshots, references taken before a write may be invalidated, and identity is not stable across writes.

When using COW fork(), prefer posix_spawn() or immediate exec() for short-lived children; set vm.overcommit_memory=1 on Linux for Redis-style BGSAVE workloads; monitor PSS (not RSS) via /proc/[pid]/smaps to account for shared pages accurately.

In COW filesystems (ZFS/Btrfs), match recordsize to the application's I/O unit (e.g., recordsize=8K for Postgres); use chattr +C (nodatacow) on Btrfs only when the fragmentation cost of random DB writes outweighs the loss of checksumming and snapshot protection.
Guard the detach + write sequence with compare_exchange or a lock when multiple threads can acquire references concurrently; a plain use_count() == 1 check is stale the moment it returns.
In persistent/functional data structures, prefer structural sharing (path-copying to root) over flat COW to keep updates O(log n) instead of O(n) for large collections.

Be aware of GC + COW interaction: avoid forking language runtimes with active mark-and-sweep collectors when the child will do meaningful work; pre-fork when the heap is cold, or use an IPC-based architecture instead. In Python, call gc.freeze() immediately before fork and gc.disable() as early as possible in the parent to minimize post-fork COW pressure.

Disable Transparent Huge Pages (THP) on hosts running forking workloads (Redis, PostgreSQL): echo never > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled. THP inflates COW granularity from 4KB to 2MB per page, amplifying fork latency and memory pressure by 512x.

For LMDB-style COW B-trees, batch writes into transactions to amortize path-copy cost: a transaction touching many keys shares the path copies, dramatically reducing write amplification vs per-key commits.
In Swift, use the _modify accessor pattern instead of manual ensureUniqueStorage() boilerplate: the compiler emits the uniqueness check automatically when using _modify.
In Rust Cow, prefer borrows on the read path (Cow::Borrowed) and only call to_mut() when mutation is confirmed needed; avoid calling to_mut() speculatively.

For Python multiprocessing with fork, set the start method to forkserver or spawn to avoid COW overhead; if fork is required, call gc.freeze() before the fork and consider gc.disable() in the parent to keep pre-fork pages cold and shareable.

When implementing custom COW in C#, use ImmutableInterlocked.Update or Interlocked.CompareExchange to atomically check-and-clone in multi-threaded scenarios; a simple if (Interlocked.Decrement(ref count) == 0) pattern is racy.

Audit all code paths that iterate a COW collection for modification during iteration: CopyOnWriteArrayList iterators are weakly consistent and will not reflect concurrent additions, which can be a surprise if the loop expects to see newly added items.

related_patterns_notes.thread-safe-copy-on-write: Extends COW with atomic reference counts or locks for cross-thread sharing; Java CopyOnWriteArrayList and Rust Arc::make_mut are canonical implementations.
related_patterns_notes.intrusive-reference-counting: COW often uses an intrusive reference count embedded in the shared body; the count is the sharing state that drives the detach decision.
related_patterns_notes.smart-pointer: shared_ptr and Arc are the handle half of COW; Arc::make_mut is the detach trigger. Rust Rc::make_mut and Arc::make_mut are COW-specific smart pointer operations.
related_patterns_notes.immutability: COW only makes sense when the shared body is effectively immutable from the outside; immutability guarantees that reads never need synchronization and that the shared state is safe.
related_patterns_notes.flyweight: Both reduce memory by sharing representation, but flyweight extracts a small token from a large intrinsic body, while COW defers the extraction to the write boundary. Structural sharing in persistent collections is a hybrid.
related_patterns_notes.lazy-initialization: COW's detach is a form of lazy initialization: the clone is deferred until the first actual write, just as a lazily-initialized object is deferred until first access.
related_patterns_notes.copy-and-swap: Often used together: a COW detach produces a private copy, which is then swapped into place; the swap commits the mutation atomically.
related_patterns_notes.snapshot-isolation: COW naturally provides snapshot isolation: readers see the frozen shared body, and writers see a private copy, exactly the MVCC guarantee. LMDB, Postgres MVCC, and CopyOnWriteArrayList are concrete instantiations.
related_patterns_notes.persistent-data-structures: Persistent collections (Clojure vectors, Scala immutable.Map, Haskell data) use structural sharing where unchanged subtrees are COW-shared between versions. Path-copying to the root is the COW descendant; the distinction is that persistent DS shares at the tree-node level, not the buffer level.
related_patterns_notes.multiversion-concurrency-control: MVCC is the database-world term for COW applied to row versions; Postgres, LMDB, CockroachDB all write new row versions (COW) and reclaim old ones via vacuum. COW B-trees provide natural snapshot isolation at the index level.
related_patterns_notes.structural-sharing: The descendant of COW for aggregate types: instead of sharing one flat buffer, individual sub-trees or sub-structures are shared between versions. Immer (C++), Immutable.js, and Scala's persistent collections use this. O(log n) update cost vs O(n) for flat COW.
related_patterns_notes.shadow-paging: The classic database term for COW at the page/block level: instead of overwriting a page in place, a new page is written and the parent pointer is atomically updated. ZFS, Btrfs, LMDB, and System R's early MVCC all use this. Equivalent to COW B-tree path copying.
